title: Writing at the Piano
intro: The piano can play bass, harmony and melody at once, which makes it a complete songwriting instrument. Most piano accompaniment comes from a few left-hand and right-hand patterns combined in different ways.

blocks.text: Keep the left hand low and open (root, root–fifth or octaves, below about C3) and the right hand in the middle (three- or four-note chords around middle C), leaving room above for a singer. Move the right hand by the smallest steps between chords, using inversions (see Inversions and Figured Bass (#/arts/music-theory/chords/inversions)): C (C E G) → F (C F A) → G (B D G) → C keeps the hand almost still.

items: Block chords: whole chords on each beat or in a rhythm. Simple and strong; the basis of most pop and rock piano.
Broken chords and arpeggios: the chord notes one at a time, rising and falling. Soft and flowing; ballads.
Alberti bass: low–high–middle–high (C G E G), the Classical left-hand pattern.
Ballad left hand: root, then fifth and octave above (C–G–C), with a sustained right-hand chord.
Stride: bass note on beats 1 and 3, chord in the middle of the keyboard on 2 and 4. Ragtime and early jazz; the 'oom-pah' of piano.
Pop pumping: right-hand chords in steady eighth notes, left hand on roots or octaves, accents on the backbeat.
Find a progression with the left hand only, then sing over it before adding the right hand; a sparse accompaniment makes melody ideas easier to hear.
Use the right hand's top note as a counter-melody: choose inversions so the top voice moves by step, and it becomes a second tune under the vocal.
Try a pedal bass (one note held under changing chords: C under C, F/C, G/C) for intros and bridges.
Change only the voicing between sections: closed, low chords in the verse, open, high ones in the chorus.

blocks.title: Inversions
blocks.text: Find right-hand voicings for Am–F–C–G that move as little as possible, starting from A C E.
solution: Am: A C E. F shares A and C: A C F (move E up to F). C shares C: G C E (A down to G, F down to E). G shares G: G B D (C down to B, E down to D). Every move is a step or a common tone.
blocks.answer: A C E → A C F → G C E → G B D

blocks.text: Sources: Perricone, J. (2018). Great Songwriting Techniques. Oxford University Press; Levine, M. (1995). The Jazz Theory Book. Sher Music; Kostka, S., Payne, D. & Almén, B. (2018). Tonal Harmony, 8th ed. McGraw-Hill.
